newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FORECAST-BIL first half profit seen lower.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-BIL first half profit seen lower.

text.p: Brierley Investments Ltd is expected to report sharply lower first half net earnings of about NZ$100-110 million on Thursday, down from $170 million a year ago, but analysts say the corporate raider's intrinsic value is on the up and its profits are of limited concern.

"With BIL, earnings aren't really the force that drives the company's valuation, and on that front, we estimate that the market value of their assets is about NZ$1.46 (per share)," said Raymond Webb, analyst at ANZ Securities.

Webb said BIL's net tangible asset backing had climbed steadily this year on the back of a big improvement in the share prices of Thistle Hotels, in which BIL has a 46 percent stake, and its three Australian holdings: John Fairfax, Coles Myer and James Hardie.
BIL shares have recently been trading at around $1.40, their highest level in over five months.
This is despite poor recent results from some of the companies it is invested in, which point to a substantially lower trading contribution this year.

"I would expect, given the well-publicised slow-down in the domestic economy and the poor interim results from Air New Zealand and Tasman Agriculture, that the trading contribution is going to be disappointing," said Webb.
Air New Zealand, in which BIL has a 42 percent stake, reported a $76.74 million interim profit last month, down 43 percent from $135.1 million a year earlier.
Tasman Agriculture, 72.57 percent owned by BIL, also showed a sharp profit decline last month when it posted a $209,000 half-year result against $1.58 million.
Casino operator Sky City Ltd reported an $18.2 million interim profit on Monday, but BIL's half share of the booty won't significantly lift total earnings.
"Also there was an absence of realised investment gains in the first half, which means that the investment contribution is not going to be high either," Webb said.
Warren Couillault, analyst at SBC Warburg, said BIL's real profits were made when it sold an investment, and its present concern was most likely what to sell next.

"Probably the thing they're thinking is 'what are we going to do at the moment?', because they're sitting on a good profit on Thistle, they're sitting on a good profit on Coles Myer, even on Fairfax, and a great big profit on Sky City," he said.
"They need to report a good profit at some stage this year, which means one of those things has to be sold."
By way of example, he said BIL's investment in Sky City was in the books at about $110 million, but the market value of the stake was roughly $360 million.
"So there's a big profit there, but they don't actually get the profit until they sell it," he said.
BIL has been building its investments in Australia.

It intends to raise its 20 percent stake in Fairfax under Australia's creep provisions, which allow it to buy three percent every six months, and has also been slowly increasing its shareholding in Coles Myer to the current level of 7.4 percent.
BIL owns 27.23 percent of James Hardie.

"They only really want to sell investments that are big or, more importantly, they have a profit on. In that case, at the moment you've really only got Sky, Coles Myer, James Hardie and Thistle," Couillault said.

Analysts said BIL was in good shape despite the expected lower profit. "A lot of their investments are coming right or running hot, and really when that happens, the (BIL) share price tracks that," Couillault said.
